newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Japan foreign minister urges infotech deal at WTO.
newsitem.headline: Japan foreign minister urges infotech deal at WTO.

text.p: Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda on Tuesday urged World Trade Organisation (WTO) members to forge a deal to scrap tariffs on a host of information technologies as well as include investment and competition issues on the global trade body's future agenda.

"On the elimination of tariffs in the area of information technology, which can be regarded as the basic infrastructure for the future industry, known as ITA, I ardently hope that we will have an agreement as the most significant achievement of this ministerial conference in the area of trade liberalisation," Ikeda said in a prepared speech.
Ministers from the 128-member Geneva-based WTO are meeting in Singapore to prepare a blueprint for free trade into the 21st century and to set the global trade watchdog's future agenda.

Japan's aspirations to play a high-profile role at the first ministerial conference of the multilateral body, whose importance it has loudly touted, have been hampered by the absence of Trade Minister Shinji Sato.
Sato was forced to stay at home to face questions in parliament about a scandal linking bureaucrats at his ministry to an oil wholesaler arrested for tax evasion.

Ikeda, who arrived before dawn on Tuesday -- the second day of the five-day conference -- said it was important not only for the WTO to ensure full implementation of the results of the Uruguay Round trade accord, but to show commitment to further liberalisation and address new issues relating to trade.
"Japan is proposing that the work relating to 'trade and investment' and 'trade and competition policy' should be initiated in the WTO as new challenges for the future," he said.

Efforts to forge an agreement on scrapping infotech tariffs have taken centre stage at the WTO meeting, with Japan strongly backing the U.S.-led initiative to open up the huge and fast-growing market.
Japan and the United States together account for over a third of the world's exports of information technology products, which the WTO estimates amounted to nearly $600 billion in 1995.

The Big Four trade partners -- the United States, Japan, the European Union and Canada -- have been trying to forge a draft deal amongst themselves while urging developing countries, especially Asian-Pacific nations, to join.

The United States last month won reluctant backing for a deal from members of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, many of them exporters of IT products, but the wording of that support was vague.
The EU, meanwhile, says it wants an infotech pact but wants it to deal with non-tariff barriers that might impede trade even if tariffs were scrapped, Japanese officials say.

Japan on Monday met with about eight Asian countries including key members of ASEAN (Association of South East Asian Nations) as well as South Korea and Hong Kong to pitch its case for an ITA, a Japanese trade official said late on Monday.

The senior official said he was "greatly encouraged" on Monday by APEC members' desire to respect last month's ITA endorsement. But he said some developing countries remained strongly opposed to expanding the WTO agenda to include investment and competition policy.
Ikeda also reiterated Japan's support for the prompt accession of China and other economies now in the process of application to the WTO.

Ikeda will hold two-way talks later on Tuesday with Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky and EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan, as well as Singapore's Trade Minister Yeo Cheow Tong. The Big Four ministers will then meet over lunch at the invitation of the EU's Brittan.
Japanese officials, somewhat embarrassed by their trade minister's failure to attend, said on Monday that Ikeda may extend his stay, originally scheduled to end late on Tuesday.
